questions.prompt: Why classify assets into tiers?
options: So protection matches each asset's real value
So nobody needs to protect public assets
So assets can be sold off by their tier
So every asset gets exactly the same protection

questions.prompt: Which tier means no harm if anyone sees it?
Which tier means severe harm if exposed or lost?
A crew-only memo that would cause mild harm if leaked is which tier?
A public recruiting flyer is locked in the starmap vault "to be safe". What is wrong?
options: Effort is wasted on what needs none
The vault is too small to hold the flyer
The flyer is not protected well enough there
Public assets must always be destroyed

questions.prompt: An internal document starts containing sensitive data. What should happen?
options: Review its tier; it may become confidential
Move it to the public tier straight away
Delete it so nobody can read it at all
Nothing, a tier is set once and kept forever

questions.prompt: What does a physical vulnerability assessment do?
options: Scans the network for open ports and services
Restores the site from a recent backup
Checks every password against a standard
Walks the site like an intruder would

questions.prompt: A propped-open emergency exit falls under which area?
A two-meter blind spot no camera covers falls under which area?
A window that does not lock falls under which area?
Which findings should be fixed first?
What sets a finding's severity?
options: How easily it could be used and the damage it would do
How many people walk past it during a normal day
How much the fix would cost the crew to put in place
How long it took the assessor to notice it on the walk

questions.prompt: Which is one of the four site selection factors?
A site has great sightlines but sits in a flood basin with one supply line. Is it a good choice?
options: Yes, floods are not a security concern
No, sightlines are the only factor
Yes, good sightlines make up for the rest
No, one bad factor can rule a site out

questions.prompt: What does approach visibility ask?
options: Can cameras record in colour at night?
Can guards see someone before they arrive?
Can visitors see the site from very far away?
Can staff see their screens in bright light?

questions.prompt: Why is one power line into a site a risk?
options: It makes the site too bright
Cutting it cuts the site off

questions.prompt: Why use biometrics for the most sensitive spaces?
options: They let many people share one entry
They work without any power at all
They are cheaper than any badge system
They can't be lost, lent or stolen

questions.prompt: Why is a badge system better than a shared key for staff areas?
options: Badges open every door in the site
Each card ties entry to one person
Keys cannot be copied by anyone
Badges never need to be revoked

questions.prompt: A crew member reports their access card missing. When should it be revoked?
A lost credential was a shared door code. What else must happen?
What is physical intrusion detection for?
options: Choosing where to build a new site
Noticing a breach when locks fail
Stopping every intruder at the door
Replacing locks on every single door

questions.prompt: A camera records, but nobody ever watches it or responds. What is the problem?
options: Cameras are a form of prevention
The camera's picture quality is far too low
The camera should face the other way
Detection with no response is near useless

questions.prompt: A door has a strong lock but no camera and no alarm. What does it lack?
Which pair are different jobs a facility needs both of?
What does compliance with a physical security checklist require?
options: A claim that each item is handled
A guard who says it is fine
A promise to fix it next year

questions.prompt: A manager says the camera footage item is "basically covered". What should an auditor ask for?
Which is a typical physical security requirement on a checklist?
options: Cameras keep footage for a set minimum
Every door is painted the same colour
Every guard works exactly eight hours
Every visitor gets a free badge to keep

questions.prompt: "It's probably fine" and "here is the documented evidence" — which satisfies an audit?
options: Neither of them, in any audit

questions.prompt: Restricted areas on a checklist often require what?
options: A single shared door code for all
